title: Unit 6 test: Integration and Accumulation of Change
author: ab-3
directions: This practice test has two sections. Section I is multiple choice: Part A without a calculator and Part B with a graphing calculator. Section II is free response: Part A with a graphing calculator and Part B without one. Show your work on free-response questions; answers without supporting work may not earn full credit. Unless a question says otherwise, angles are in radians, exact answers are expected without a calculator, and calculator answers are given to three decimal places. Results are raw points for practice only.

Graph of y = f(t) for −3 ≤ t ≤ 4 made of line segments joining the points (−3, −2), (−1, 2), (1, 2), (3, −2), and (4, −2).

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: Choose the best answer. No calculator is allowed.

items.prompt:
Water flows into a tank at a rate of R(t) liters per hour, where R is continuous. Selected values are shown.

| t (h) | 0 | 1 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R(t) (L/h) | 8 | 10 | 14 | 11 |

Using a left Riemann sum with the three subintervals in the table, what is the estimate of the water that flows in from t = 0 to t = 4?
items.rationale: The widths are 1, 2, and 1 hours and the left endpoints give 8, 10, and 14 L/h: 8(1) + 10(2) + 14(1) = 42 liters.

distractorNotes.A: Adds the three left heights without multiplying by the unequal widths.
distractorNotes.C: This is the trapezoidal sum, not the left sum.

items.prompt: Which expression equals lim as n→∞ of Σ from k = 1 to n of (5/n)e^(2 + 5k/n)?
choices: ∫ from 2 to 7 of e^(2 + x) dx
items.rationale: Δx = 5/n and the sample points 2 + 5k/n run from 2 to 7, so the limit is ∫ from 2 to 7 of e^x dx.

distractorNotes.B: Keeps the width 5 but drops the starting value 2; this would need the integrand e^(2 + x).
distractorNotes.C: Uses the interval [2, 7] and also shifts the function, counting the 2 twice.
distractorNotes.D: Counts the width factor 5 a second time; dx already accounts for it.

items.prompt: If F(x) = ∫ from 0 to x^3 of 1/(1 + t^2) dt, what is F′(1)?
items.rationale: By the Fundamental Theorem and the chain rule, F′(x) = 3x^2/(1 + x^6), so F′(1) = 3/2.

distractorNotes.B: This is F(1) = arctan 1, not F′(1).
distractorNotes.D: Uses only the chain-rule factor 3x^2 and omits the integrand's value.

items.prompt: The graph of f, which consists of line segments, is shown for 0 ≤ t ≤ 7. Let g(x) = ∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt. At what value of x does g have a relative minimum on the open interval (0, 7)?
items.rationale: g′(x) = f(x), which changes from negative to positive at x = 6, so g has a relative minimum there.

distractorNotes.A: At x = 2, f changes from positive to negative, so g has a relative maximum.
distractorNotes.B: At x = 3, f reaches its lowest value; g's slope is most negative there, but g keeps decreasing.
distractorNotes.C: f is still negative just after x = 5, so g is still decreasing.

items.prompt: If ∫ from −1 to 4 of f(x) dx = 9 and ∫ from 4 to 1 of f(x) dx = 2, what is ∫ from −1 to 1 of (2f(x) − 1) dx?
items.rationale: ∫ from 1 to 4 of f = −2, so ∫ from −1 to 1 of f = 9 − (−2) = 11. Then 2(11) − ∫ from −1 to 1 of 1 dx = 22 − 2 = 20.

distractorNotes.A: Ignores the reversed limits and uses ∫ from 1 to 4 of f = 2, giving 2(7) − 2.
distractorNotes.C: Subtracts 1 instead of the integral of 1 over an interval of length 2.

items.prompt: What is ∫ from 1 to 4 of (x − 2)/√x dx?

distractorNotes.B: Subtracts in the wrong order, F(1) − F(4).
distractorNotes.C: Integrates only x/√x and drops the −2/√x term.
distractorNotes.D: Evaluates the antiderivative at the upper limit only.

items.prompt: Which is ∫ cos x/(1 + sin x)^2 dx?
items.rationale: Let u = 1 + sin x, du = cos x dx: ∫ u^(−2) du = −u^(−1) + C = −1/(1 + sin x) + C.

distractorNotes.A: Loses the negative sign from integrating u^(−2).
distractorNotes.B: Treats the integrand as a logarithmic derivative, but the numerator is not the derivative of (1 + sin x)^2.
distractorNotes.D: Lowers the exponent instead of raising it.

items.prompt: What is ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x^2 + 2)/(x^2 + 1) dx?
items.rationale: Divide: (x^2 + 2)/(x^2 + 1) = 1 + 1/(x^2 + 1). The integral is [x + arctan x] from 0 to 1 = 1 + π/4.

distractorNotes.A: Drops the quotient 1 from the division and keeps only the remainder term.
distractorNotes.B: Integrates the remainder 1/(x^2 + 1) as a logarithm.
distractorNotes.C: Integrates the numerator and denominator separately and divides the results.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Choose the best answer. A graphing calculator is required for some questions. If the exact value is not a choice, choose the closest approximation.

items.prompt: Rainwater flows into a barrel at a rate of r(t) = 30 + 12 sin(t^2/8) liters per hour for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 hours. How many liters flow into the barrel during the 6 hours?
items.rationale: The total is ∫ from 0 to 6 of r(t) dt ≈ 203.672 liters by numerical integration.

distractorNotes.D: This is r(6), a rate, not an amount.

items.prompt: Let F(x) = ∫ from 0 to x of (1 − te^(t/3)) dt. What is the maximum value of F on the interval [0, 3]?
items.rationale: F′(x) = 1 − xe^(x/3) changes from positive to negative at x ≈ 0.773, and F(0.773) ≈ 0.418 exceeds F(0) = 0 and F(3) = −6.

distractorNotes.A: This is where the maximum occurs, not its value.
distractorNotes.B: This is F′(0), the integrand's value at 0.
distractorNotes.D: This is F(3), the minimum on the interval.

items.prompt: What is the midpoint Riemann sum with four subintervals of equal width for ∫ from 0 to 2 of 1/(1 + x^3) dx?
A function f satisfies f′(x) = ln(x^2 + 2) and f(1) = 4. What is f(3)?

distractorNotes.A: Finds the net change but does not add f(1).
distractorNotes.C: Adds f′(3) to f(1) instead of the accumulated change.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: A graphing calculator is required. Show the setup for every calculator result, and give answers to three decimal places with units.

items.prompt:
Water is pumped into a greenhouse irrigation tank at a rate of P(t) liters per hour for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8 hours, where P is a differentiable function; selected values are shown in the table. Water drains out of the tank at a rate of D(t) = 30 + 10 sin(t/2) liters per hour.

| t (h) | 0 | 2 | 3 | 6 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P(t) (L/h) | 40 | 52 | 55 | 46 | 38 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals in the table to approximate ∫ from 0 to 8 of P(t) dt. Write out the sum you use.

rubric.criterion: Uses the widths 2, 1, 3, 2 with averaged endpoint values.

steps: The subintervals have unequal widths, so each trapezoid uses its own width.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What does ∫ from 2 to 6 of P(t) dt measure for this tank? Give its units.

rubric.criterion: The number of liters of water pumped into the tank from t = 2 to t = 6 hours.

parts.answer: It is the total amount of water, in liters, pumped into the tank between t = 2 and t = 6 hours.
steps: P is a rate in liters per hour, so its integral over hours is liters.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Must there be a time t, 3 < t < 6, at which P′(t) = −3 liters per hour per hour? Give a reason.

rubric.criterion: Yes, by the Mean Value Theorem: P is differentiable, so it is continuous on [3, 6] and differentiable on (3, 6).

parts.answer: Yes. (P(6) − P(3))/(6 − 3) = (46 − 55)/3 = −3 liters per hour per hour. P is differentiable, so it is continuous on [3, 6] and differentiable on (3, 6), and the Mean Value Theorem gives a time t in (3, 6) with P′(t) = −3.
steps: The average rate of change of P over [3, 6] is −9/3 = −3.
The hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem hold because P is differentiable on the whole interval.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find the time T, 0 < T < 8, at which the total amount of water that has drained out of the tank since t = 0 is 150 liters.

rubric.criterion: Sets up ∫ from 0 to T of D(t) dt = 150.

parts.answer: Solving ∫ from 0 to T of (30 + 10 sin(t/2)) dt = 150 gives T ≈ 4.043 hours.
steps: The water drained from time 0 to time T is the accumulation ∫ from 0 to T of D(t) dt.
Graph it as a function of T, or use the solver, and find where it equals 150: T ≈ 4.043.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Is the amount of water in the tank increasing or decreasing at t = 6? Give a reason based on the two rates.

rubric.criterion: Uses A′(t) = P(t) − D(t) for the amount A(t) in the tank.
Computes 46 − D(6) ≈ 46 − 31.411 = 14.589 > 0 and concludes the amount is increasing.

parts.answer: Increasing: A′(6) = P(6) − D(6) ≈ 46 − 31.411 = 14.589 liters per hour > 0.
steps: A(t) = A(0) + ∫ from 0 to t of (P(s) − D(s)) ds, so by the Fundamental Theorem A′(t) = P(t) − D(t).

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: No calculator is allowed. Show your work and give exact answers.

items.prompt: The graph of the continuous function f, which consists of line segments, is shown for −3 ≤ t ≤ 4. Let g(x) = ∫ from 0 to x of f(t) dt.

parts.label: a
steps: On [−3, 0]: triangle −1 (on [−3, −2]), triangle 1 (on [−2, −1]), rectangle 2 (on [−1, 0]); reversing the limits changes the sign.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the x-coordinate of each relative extremum of g on the open interval (−3, 4), and classify each. Give a reason for each, based on the graph of f.

rubric.criterion: Relative minimum at x = −2 because g′ = f changes from negative to positive there.
Relative maximum at x = 2 because g′ = f changes from positive to negative there.

parts.answer: Relative minimum at x = −2; relative maximum at x = 2.
steps: g′(x) = f(x) by the Fundamental Theorem.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: On what open interval or intervals is the graph of g concave down? Explain how the graph of f shows this.

rubric.criterion: Reason: g″ = f′ < 0 there, because f is decreasing.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Use a substitution to evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of f(2x − 2) dx.

rubric.criterion: Changes the limits to u = −2 and u = 2 and writes (1/2)∫ from −2 to 2 of f(u) du.

steps: With u = 2x − 2, dx = du/2; x = 0 gives u = −2 and x = 2 gives u = 2.
